abstract: |
  Federal representation in Canada is geographical: one Member of Parliament represents one electoral district. Despite this, Canadians can legally donate to many political entities, regardless of proximity. Using public data from Elections Canada matched with the Canadian Census, we characterize broad patterns in Canadian out-of-district donation from 2015 to 2024. We find that out-of-district donations consistently represent around 40% of donor-sourced funding to both candidates and district associations. While relatively constant in time, the propensity for out-of-district donation varied substantially across districts. Those with higher population density, median household income, educational attainment, and visible minority proportions see higher rates of out-of-district giving - the same traits that predict donor prevalence generally. Still, donations remain regionalized; nearly half of donations that leave their district are sent to neighbouring ones, and few cross provincial lines. Our findings may inform further research into the geography of local campaign finance and effective representation in Canada. \

  **Keywords:** out-of-district donation; Canadian politics; political geography; political financing

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

<!-- Intro -->
In Canada, federal representation is structurally geographical. Citizens are grouped into a few hundred electoral districts based on where they live, each represented by a single Member of Parliament (MP), and even where the boundaries are drawn can shape which party forms government [@cochrane_boundary_2026]. An individual’s political influence in this system is canonically exercised by voting for their candidate of choice during election periods. Beyond the ballot, alternate forms of political engagement exist to support a broader scope of activities, entities, and without the spatio-temporal constraints imposed by elections. Citizens may volunteer at their local district associations, advocate for their preferred national party online, or contribute financially to a candidate’s campaign [@baker_getting_2016; @garnett_where_2024]. 

<!-- Donations are THE PP tool that breaches district borders, and a major source of campaign funding in Canada -->
Whether intentional or not, these alternative forms of political participation may serve to extend a citizen’s political influence beyond their district’s boundaries, and among these, donations are perhaps the clearest and most flexible mechanism of doing so [@gimpel_check_2008]. In Canada, citizens and permanent residents can legally contribute to a host of federal political entities at any time, in any district, and as often as they want, subject to annual and per-election limitations [@canada_annual_2026]. These political entities are tied to a specific district in a number of ways including of course the candidate seeking election in a particular district, the electoral district association (EDA), the permanent local organization (often called a "riding association") that a registered party maintains in each district to raise funds, select candidates, and support the local campaign. We consider these localized entities. Beyond their flexibility, individual donations are a major source of funding for individual constituency campaigns [@cross_money_2020; @garnett_where_2024; @canada_understanding_2026]. While campaign expenses may be partially reimbursed through public subsidies, most funds needed for a candidate to carry out an effective campaign must be available on-demand [@garnett_where_2024]. National parties do transfer funds to their candidates, but a district's local apparatus -- the candidate and their association -- is routinely expected to generate the bulk of its own funds from individual donors.

<!-- OOD and it's effects in the U.S. -->
Despite a growing body of Canadian research documenting the extent of, and patterns in, federal political donations generally [e.g. @besco_ethnic_2022; @tolley_who_2022; @garnett_where_2024], comparatively little attention has been given to out-of-district donations. Existing research in the U.S. documents substantial rates of out-of-district giving during congressional campaigns, wherein the typical House (Senate) candidate sources over two-thirds (half) of their campaign donations from out-of-district (out-of-state) [@gimpel_check_2008; @sievert_out_2023]. These donations are thought to be primarily motivated by partisan gain [@gimpel_check_2008; @jacobs_nationalization_2024], and redirect legislators' responsiveness from local constituents toward national donor bases [@baker_getting_2016; @canes_wrone_out_2022; @jacobs_nationalization_2024; @nathan_donor_2025]. Further, and to an overwhelming degree, these donations originate from a single small group of disproportionately wealthy, older, white, and well educated districts [@gimpel_political_2006; @bramlett_political_2011].

<!-- Methods and data avaliabilty statement -->
In this paper, we document the extent of, and large-scale trends in, Canadian out-of-district donations to electoral candidates and district associations from 2015 to 2024. We use a database containing all contributions received by federal political entities during this period, made publicly available by Elections Canada and pre-processed by the Investigative Journalism Foundation. This dataset was augmented by situating donors geographically, and matching donations to their socio-demographic environment using the 2021 Census, allowing us to better understand which factors correlate with out-of-district donation rates. In addition to our findings, this study contributes a cleaned, de-duplicated, and analysis-ready dataset of individual contributions to all federal political entities from 2015 to 2024, which we have made available upon request[^data-accessibility].

<!-- Results and significance -->
We find that, between 2015 and 2024, out-of-district donations account for a persistent share of donor-sourced funding to both electoral candidates and district associations, averaging roughly 40% across time, election periods, and party lines. This relative invariance does not extend to space, however. The propensity for out-of-district donation changes substantially from district to district. Donations originating from densely populated, high-income, and well-educated districts are more likely to leave their district of origin, echoing predictors of out-of-district giving established in the U.S. Our analysis also shows that the visible minority proportion of a donor's district was strongly correlated with out-of-district propensity. This departs from historically white "donor districts" of the U.S. [@gimpel_political_2006; @bramlett_political_2011; @canes_wrone_out_2022], but aligns with recent Canadian studies linking minority ethnic communities to higher rates of in- and out-of-district giving [@garnett_lifeblood_2022; @besco_ethnic_2022]. Despite the prevalence of out-of-district donations, direct donor funding remains regional: nearly half of all donations that leave their district of origin are addressed to political entities in a neighbouring one, and less than one-fifth crossed a provincial boundary, limiting their potential influence on geographically based representation.

Although we do not formally test the representational impacts of out-of-district donations, their systematic characterization presented here provides a foundation for future research on this topic, and improves understanding of the origins of local campaign finance.

[^data-accessibility]: The dataset cannot be redistributed directly, but it can be reconstructed in full by following the steps at <https://zenodo.org/records/21708656>. Doing so requires a file licensed from Canada Post [@statcan_pccf_2025], as well as a pre-processed dataset obtained on request from the Investigative Journalism Foundation.

# Background {#sec-lit}

## Out-of-district Donation in the U.S. and its Representational Effects  {#sec-lit-motivation}

<!-- U.S. structural context and problem statement -->   
Our study is motivated by existing research on out-of-district donations to U.S. members of Congress (representatives and senators). There, members of both chambers formally represent, and are elected by citizens living in geographically defined regions of the country (districts and states, respectively). Like in Canada, individual constituency campaigns are funded in large part by individual donors [@ansolabehere_why_2003; @corrado_new_2010; @barber_donation_2016], which need not reside in their constituency. U.S. scholars describe big donors and their environments as wealthy, older, white, and well-educated [@francia_financiers_2003; @mandle_funding_2007; @gimpel_political_2006], characteristics which are decidedly unrepresentative of the typical U.S. voter [@bonica_democracy_2013; @hill_representativeness_2017; @grumbach_race_2020].  Given this, and broader trends in the "nationalization" of campaign finance [@hopkins_nationalization_2018;  @sievert_out_2023; @jacobs_nationalization_2024], recent U.S. literature has sought to (1) document rates of out-of-district donation, and (2) test whether such donations warp the classically "dyadic" [@weissberg_collective_1978] member–constituent relationship  in favour of "surrogate" [@mansbridge_rethinking_2003] representatives; legislators more responsive to their national donor base.

<!-- Descriptive findings -->
Research describing nationalized donations and donor characteristics during electoral campaigns in the U.S. is not new [@francia_financiers_2003; @mandle_funding_2007; @gimpel_political_2006]. However, it can be argued that @gimpel_check_2008's examination of out-of-district donations during four Congressional elections between 1994 and 2004 catalyzed research on out-of-district donations and their representational effects. During this period, the typical candidate received roughly two-thirds of individual donations from out-of-district, a rate reproduced for more recent elections by @canes_wrone_out_2022. For both Republican and Democrat candidates, a large majority of these donations originated from a shared set of so-called "donor districts": a small number of wealthy, educated, older, and affluent districts. Notably, these socio-demographic predictors are largely identical to those predicting a region's donor output in general [@gimpel_political_2006]. Because district competitiveness strongly predicts the share of donor funding received from out-of-district, they argue that this behaviour is primarily motivated by partisan advantage. More recent studies on out-of-state donations to Senate candidates report out-of-state donation shares over 50%, which have increased steadily over the century, for both parties [@jacobs_nationalization_2024; @sievert_out_2023; @keena_out_2024].

<!-- Representational Impacts -->
Beyond descriptions of the phenomenon, U.S. literature on out-of-district donations offers strong evidence that these contributions have tangible representational effects. @bramlett_political_2011 pair national donation and survey data to show that donors from @gimpel_check_2008's  "donor districts" have a unique political ecology distinct from other parts of the country, which likely intensifies bias in opinion. @baker_getting_2016 study the 2006-2010 Congressional elections, revealing that representatives become less responsive to their constituencies’ ideological preferences when heavily reliant on out-of-district contributions. @canes_wrone_out_2022 further explore the 2006-2016 Congressional elections to show that House voting behaviour is indeed associated with the preferences of their national donor base, contrasted against earlier research finding that political action committees (PACs) do not affect roll call behaviour [@ansolabehere_why_2003]. Studies on Senatorial elections also argue that out-of-state-donations have meaningful representational impacts [@jacobs_nationalization_2024]. For instance, @nathan_donor_2025 experimentally demonstrate that constituents who learned about outside donation expected their senators to be less loyal to local interests, emphasizing the rivalrous relationship that may form between local constituents and national donor bases.

## Individual Donations and Campaign Financing in Canada {#sec-lit-review}

<!-- Why research hasn't been done in Canada at scale -->
Few studies[^notable-exception] analyze out-of-district donation shares to Canadian parliamentary candidates, or electoral district associations (EDAs). We propose three potential reasons why. Most obviously, U.S. campaign financing moves vastly more money, and sustains a larger research community which has recently been interested in the nationalization of campaign finance. Second, location-disclosed donations in the U.S. (those whose donors gave over \$200) account for an overwhelming majority of individual donor funding [@corrado_new_2010]. While Canadian donors who have contributed over $200 must also disclose their location [@canada_understanding_2026], contribution limits are stricter than in the U.S., so smaller, location-anonymized donations make up a larger share of donor-based funding to federal political entities overall. Third, Canadian contributions records are not presented in an analysis-ready format: the researcher must situate donors within districts and dissemination areas manually, and records are often duplicated since big databases often merge Annual, Quarterly, and Electoral financial returns [@canada_open_2025].

<!-- Direct individual donations (DIDs) are important + the place of DIDs is campaign finance -->
This lack of research is not, however, a signal that direct individual donations are an unimportant piece of Canadian campaign financing. District campaigns are run by candidates, with financial support from their electoral district associations[^independent-candidates-disclaimer]. Together, these entities receive the majority[^funding-disclaimer] of their combined funding from three[^reimbursement-disclaimer] sources: individual contributions (limited to \$1775 per contributor[^limit-disclaimer]), unlimited transfers from their affiliated central party, and unlimited transfers to the EDA from other EDAs [@cross_money_2020; @curriewood_interEDA_2020; @canada_elections_act]. While in principle this funding scheme allows local entities to source most of its funds directly from the central party, in practice, this is rarely the case. For instance, during the 2015 general election period, central party transfers supplied roughly one-quarter of campaign funding[^coletto-substantiation], and inter-EDA transfers less than ten percent [@cross_money_2020]. Local campaign reliance on individual funds is consistent with the established "stratarchical" organization of Canadian parties and party finance [@carty_politics_2002; @coletto_stratarchical_2011; @cross_money_2020]. While national parties exert undeniable influence over their local district campaigns, scholars note that Canadian parties have decentralized candidate selection processes, and a high tolerance for personalized campaigns tackling local issues [@cross_personalization_2015].  

[^notable-exception]: A notable counterexample is @besco_ethnic_2022, discussed later in this section. 

[^coletto-substantiation]: Similar proportions were found in @coletto_stratarchical_2011's study of campaign finance. In both studies, campaigns from all three major Canadian parties sourced, at most, 30% of their funding from the central party.

[^reimbursement-disclaimer]: Candidates that received at least 10% of votes are eligible to have 60% of their election expenses reimbursed through public subsidies [@canada_expenses_2026]. While an important source of funding, we feel that these do not undermine the importance of individual contributions, since they are not available up-front.

[^limit-disclaimer]: This limit applies on an annual basis for district associations, and a per-election basis for candidates [@canada_understanding_2026]. \$1775 CAD is accurate as of 2026, and increases by \$25 CAD every year. 

[^funding-disclaimer]: We are assuming that other legal transfers (e.g. transfers from leadership contestants, nomination contestants) are negligible for the average district association or candidate.

[^independent-candidates-disclaimer]: Non-partisan (i.e. independent) candidates do not have EDAs, and are therefore funded up-front entirely by individual donors. 

<!-- Existing research on donor characteristics in Canada -->
Existing research on Canadian donations has described who donates to electoral candidates[^other-entity-donations], beginning with constituency-level analysis of campaign contributions by @eagles_political_1992. Initial analyses of individual donations from 2006 to 2011 [@jansen_donates_2012; @carmichael_political_2014], and a more recent analysis of candidate-bound donations during the 2015, 2019, and 2021 general elections [@garnett_where_2024] have found that donors are more likely to originate from older, wealthier, and better-educated districts. @garnett_where_2024 in particular finds also that donations are more likely to originate from regions with higher visible minority proportions. Survey-based studies by @tolley_who_2022 and @mcmahon_covid_2023 find that women are less likely to donate than men. These socio-demographic characteristics are similar to those attributed to U.S. donors, with the exception of ethnicity.

Related studies suggest that Canadian donors are more likely to donate to candidates with whom they share aspects of their identity with. For instance, women donors are more likely to donate to women candidates [@tolley_who_2022], and rates of co-ethnic donation are high, particularly among South Asian donors [@besco_ethnic_2022]. Another study analyzing donor-candidate co-ethnic affinity reports that the likelihood of a donor donating out-of-district is higher for ethnic minorities (50 - 70%) compared to donors of European origin (33%) [@besco_ethnic_2022].

[^other-entity-donations]: We refer the reader to @young_money_2011, @garnett_lifeblood_2022, @pruysers_leadership_2024, and @mockler_nominationFundraising_2024 for Canadian-context studies on contributions to other political entities.


# Data and Methods {#sec-data}

## Overview of Data Acquisition and Processing {#sec-data-overview}

<!-- Overview of primary dataset in full -->
The data used in this paper was originally sourced from the Elections Canada Open Data on Contributions datasets [@canada_open_2025]. Since 2004, the *Canada Elections Act* has required that all individual contributions to federal political entities[^contributions-disclaimer] valued at over \$20 be recorded by the recipient, shared with the government, and made publicly accessible [@canada_understanding_2026]. In addition, donors whose cumulative sum of contributions exceeds \$200 are required to disclose their full name and address, including their postal code. For all contributions, Elections Canada also records the receiving political entity's name, district affiliation (if applicable), party (if applicable), type (e.g. national party, candidate, etc.), and the date the contribution was received. The primary dataset used in this study is a pre-processed version of Elections Canada's, made available to us by the Investigative Journalism Foundation. Their cleaning process is described in Supplement {{< meta supp.pipeline >}}.

[^contributions-disclaimer]: Donations (monetary or otherwise), loans, and loan guarantees received by national parties, EDAs, leadership contestants, nomination contestants, and electoral candidates are regulated by the *Act*. 

<!-- Statement of entity focus -->
To even be considered out-of-district, a federal donation must be received by a political entity that is representationally tied to a specific district. For this reason, our study primarily focuses on donations sent to candidates (during election periods) and district associations[^nomination-and-by-elections], hereafter referred to as localized entities. However, given the prevalence of donations sent to national entities (parties or leadership contestants), we briefly compare them with those addressed to localized entities in @sec-data-summaries.

[^nomination-and-by-elections]: Nomination contestants and by-electioral candidates are also tied to specific districts. Due to the relative scarcity of donations addressed to these, they were not considered in this analysis.

<!-- Our major restrictions + how OOD assessments were made -->
Every ten years, federal electoral district (FED) boundaries are redrawn to account for population changes that occurred within the decade [@canada_redistribution_2025]. To restrict our focus to a single, static set of FEDs, our analysis only includes contributions made during the 2013 representational order, effective between October 2, 2015 and April 22, 2024 [@canada_redistribution_2025]. This is the largest order present in the dataset, capturing 61% of all recorded contributions since 2004, and spanning three general election periods (42nd, 43rd, and 44th). Donors were matched to their FEDs by their postal codes using Statistics Canada's Postal Code Conversion Files[^PC-to-FED] [@statcan_pccf_2025], made available to us by the University of Toronto. Donor FEDs were then compared with recipient FEDs to assess whether a donation was out-of-district. Donor location was not recorded for the majority of donations under \$200, and the small share that could be geolocated were distributed very differently from the rest of the data. For these reasons, this study only considers donations above \$200, as was done in similar studies [@gimpel_check_2008; @garnett_where_2024]. Smaller donations are discussed further in Supplement {{< meta supp.missing-data >}}.

<!-- Census augmentation -->
Postal codes were also used to situate donors within census dissemination areas (DA), allowing us to attribute socio-demographic characteristics to their environments at a fine spatial grain. For each dissemination area, we identified its population density, median household income, mean age, proportion of the population with a post-secondary education, and proportions of various visible minority ethnicities. A full list of the ethnicities we consider is available in Supplement {{< meta supp.supplement-data >}}. These variables were informed by similar studies on donor demography [@gimpel_political_2006 ; @gimpel_check_2008 ; @garnett_where_2024]. Further, ethnicities were disaggregated since previous Canadian research has found that some minority groups such as South Asians donate at much higher rates than others [@besco_ethnic_2022]. We again used Postal Code Conversion Files to match donor postal codes to the DAs of the 2021 Census, and to group DAs into FEDs[^DA-to-FED] to deduce the same socio-demographic information at the district level.

[^PC-to-FED]: Postal codes may straddle multiple FEDs. For this study, we created a deterministic spatial lookup table that resolves these cases using reasonable criteria. Donations whose postal codes could not be matched in this way were dropped. Our methodologies, and loss impact assessments are detailed further in Supplement {{< meta supp.supplement-data >}}..

[^DA-to-FED]: Dissemination areas may straddle multiple FEDs. Supplement {{< meta supp.supplement-data >}} discusses how these cases were handled.

<!-- Candidate/competitiveness information + Data statement -->
Finally, we obtained data on election outcomes and candidate traits for each race in the 42nd, 43rd, and 44th general elections. Election outcomes (in particular, margins of victory) were used as proxies for race competitiveness, and were sourced from Open Government Canada [@canada_open_government_2026]. Candidate traits such as gender, ethnicity, LGBTQ2S+ status, and incumbency were sourced from @baisley_dataset_2026. We discuss how these data are used in further sections. A detailed walkthrough of the full data pipeline, from the files available for download on Canadian government websites to the core datasets used for analysis can be found in Supplement {{< meta supp.pipeline >}}. and Supplement {{< meta supp.supplement-data >}}. All data cleaning, validation, visualization, and analysis was conducted using the R statistical software [@r_citation].

## Data Summaries {#sec-data-summaries}

<!-- Data Summaries Sections:
      - Situating Localized Donations.                UOI: the localized donation (amount and count)
      - Trends in Out-of-district Donation Rates.     UOI: Pr(is_out_of_district) ; share that leaves the district
      - Characterizing Inter-District Funding Flows.  UOI: ONLY out-of-district donations
-->

### Situating Localized Donations {#sec-data-summaries-situation}

<!-- DECISION: In TS plots, keeping Fiscal-assigned donation dates. Doesn't matter for analysis or models. -->

We first provide summaries of all donations[^contribution-donation-inter] during our study period, to help situate further analysis of out-of-district donations to localized entities. @tbl-data-summaries-situation breaks down donations by recipient type. Parties and leadership contestants received the majority (80.8%) of contributions during our study period. Among donations addressed to localized entities, 24.3% are received by candidates, and 75.7% were received by district associations (EDAs). During election periods, donations to candidates formed 48% of the funding received by localized entities, with district associations making up the remaining 52% (Supplement {{< meta supp.extra-viz >}}.).

@fig-data-summaries-situation-timelines shows how contributions during our study period were distributed in time[^time-disclaimer], for national and localized entities separately. Among national-level donations, we observe three distinct temporal signatures. First, donation rates are higher in December of every year during our study, likely since charitable donations tend to be more common in this period in general, as individuals claim tax deductions and give more during the holidays. Second, we observe six peaks corresponding to general election periods (peaks during and immediately before grey shaded regions), and Conservative party leadership campaigns (peaks in the blue trend line in the first half of 2017, 2020, and 2022). Third, national-entity donation rates generally increased over our study period, following trends observed from 2004 to 2015 by @mcmahon_follow_2015, and particularly following the 2021 general election in the Conservative party.

Donation rates to localized entities exhibited the same December and election period peaks that were observed for donations to national entities, however an increasing trend was not observed. This agrees with trends observed in candidate-bound donations by @garnett_where_2024 and @canada_report_2026 over similar periods. We also observe a significant reduction in donations to EDAs from the start of 2019 to mid-2021. This may in part be attributed to the COVID-19 pandemic [@mcmahon_covid_2023], however it is not entirely clear why donations to district associations do not appear in our dataset during this period. Simple spatial comparisons between the donor bases of national and localized entities during our study period yielded only minor differences, and are presented in Supplement {{< meta supp.extra-viz >}}..

[^contribution-donation-inter]: From @sec-data onwards, the terms "donation" and "contribution" are used interchangeably and implicitly refer to individual contributions above $200 that were successfully donor-geolocated.
[^time-disclaimer]: All donations to electoral candidates and leadership contestants were tied to specific events in time. A small proportion (0.7% of the total contributed amount) of contributions to EDAs and national parties over \$200 were missing specific dates, but could always be attributed to a fiscal year. Plots over time in this report include these cases, which slightly exaggerates the observed December peaks in contribution rates. 

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-data-summaries-situation
#| tbl-cap: "Breakdown of contributions over $200 to major Canadian federal political entities, from 2015 to 2024. Nomination contestants and by-electoral candidates are excluded from this Table."

# Create Table
grand_total_amount <- sum(donations_data$total_amount)

Tbl_data_summaries_situation <- donations_data %>%
  mutate(`Political Entity` =  case_when(
    political_entity == "Registered parties" ~ "Party",
    political_entity == "Leadership contestants" ~ "Leadership Contestant",
    political_entity == "Candidates" ~ "Candidate",
    political_entity == "Registered associations" ~ "District Association",
  )) %>%
  mutate(Type = ifelse(is_local, "Localized", "National")) %>%
  group_by(`Political Entity`) %>%
  summarise(
    Type = Type[1],
    `Donation Count` = n(),
    `Donation Amount (Thousands)` = sum(total_amount) / 1000,
    `Share of Total Amount` = sum(total_amount) / grand_total_amount
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    `Donation Count` = scales::comma(`Donation Count`),
    `Donation Amount (Thousands)` = scales::dollar(`Donation Amount (Thousands)`, accuracy = 1),
    `Share of Total Amount` = scales::percent(`Share of Total Amount`, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) %>%
  tinytable::tt(width = 1) %>%
  format_tt(escape = TRUE) %>%
  style_tt(j = 1:5, align = "llrrr") %>%
  style_tt(i = 0:nrow(.), fontsize = 0.85) %>%
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)

# Display Table
Tbl_data_summaries_situation
```

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-data-summaries-situation-timelines
#| fig-cap: "Time series of contributions above $200 to national (A) and localized (B) federal political entities from 2015 to 2024. Within each panel, trendlines are separated by the party of the recipient. Shaded vertical bars indicate the 42nd, 43rd, and 44th general election periods respectively. Series were qualitatively similar when contributions under $200 were included."
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 6.5

timeline_panel <- function(data, panel_title) {
  data %>%
    mutate(
      political_party = factor(
        if_else(political_party %in% PARTIES_NAMED, political_party, "Other"),
        levels = names(PARTY_COLOURS)
      ),
      month = lubridate::floor_date(donation_date, "month")
    ) %>%
    group_by(month, political_party) %>%
    summarise(total_donated = sum(total_amount), n_donors = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = month, y = total_donated / 1e6, color = political_party)) +
    geom_rect(
      data = ELECTION_PERIODS,
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
      fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.5
    ) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_color_manual(values = PARTY_COLOURS) +
    scale_x_date(
      date_breaks = "1 year",
      date_minor_breaks = "1 month",
      date_labels = "%Y",
      guide = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE)
    ) +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = "Monthly Donation Total (in millions of dollars)",
      color = NULL,
      title = panel_title
    ) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
      legend.position = "top",

      axis.minor.ticks.length.x.bottom = rel(0.6),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 6),
      legend.key.size = grid::unit(5, "mm")
    )
}

panel_a <- timeline_panel(filter(donations_data, !is_local), "A. National entities")
panel_b <- timeline_panel(filter(donations_data, is_local), "B. Localized entities")

(panel_a / panel_b) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
```

### Spatio-temporal Trends in Out-of-district Donation Rates {#sec-data-summaries-ood-rate}

In this section, we present data summaries describing when and where out-of-district contributions are more or less common.  @tbl-data-summaries-ood-rate-overall displays the proportion of donations above $200 (raw and amount-weighted) that were sent out-of-district, for donations to candidates and EDAs. Overall, candidates received 37.6% of their donations from outside their district, and EDAs received 43.8%. In both cases, these proportions increase when donations are weighed by their value, indicating that out-of-district donations are larger, on average, than their within-district counterparts. 

@tbl-data-summaries-ood-rate-candidates and @fig-data-summaries-ood-rate-EDAs[^trendline] show how out-of-district funding rates change over time, for candidates and district associations respectively. Rates for candidates show a slight decreasing trend, from 39.5% in the 42nd general election in 2015 to around 35.4% in subsequent periods (@tbl-data-summaries-ood-rate-candidates). However, this may reflect the heightened absolute number of contributions received in 2015, due to that election's unusually long writ-period. EDAs received roughly the same proportion of out-of-district contributions during the entire study period, including during writ periods[^party-EDA-OOD-rates].

[^trendline]: We emphasize the trend instead of raw shares to control for large month-to-month variation in donation
rates to EDAs (shown in @fig-data-summaries-situation-timelines).

[^party-EDA-OOD-rates]: Roughly similar rates, and the same consistency through time, were observed when entities from individual parties were examined (Supplement {{< meta supp.extra-viz >}}).

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-data-summaries-ood-rate-overall
#| tbl-cap: "Proportion of contributions over $200 to candidates (excluding by-elections) and district associations that were received from outside their district, from 2015 to 2024."

# Create Table
Tbl_data_summaries_ood_rate_overall <- localized_donations_data %>%
  mutate(`Political Entity` = ifelse(political_entity == "Candidates", "Candidate", "District Association")) %>%
  group_by(`Political Entity`) %>%
  summarise(
    `Donation Count` = n(),
    `Donation Amount (Thousands)` = sum(total_amount) / 1000,
    `OOD Proportion` = mean(is_out_of_district),
    `OOD Proportion (Amount Weighted)` = sum(is_out_of_district * total_amount) / sum(total_amount)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    `Donation Count` = scales::comma(`Donation Count`),
    `Donation Amount (Thousands)` = scales::dollar(`Donation Amount (Thousands)`, accuracy = 1),
    `OOD Proportion` = scales::percent(`OOD Proportion`, accuracy = 0.1),
    `OOD Proportion (Amount Weighted)` = scales::percent(`OOD Proportion (Amount Weighted)`, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) %>%
  tinytable::tt(width = 1) %>%
  format_tt(escape = TRUE) %>%
  style_tt(j = 1:5, align = "llrrr") %>%
  style_tt(i = 0:nrow(.), fontsize = 0.85) %>%
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)

# Display Table
Tbl_data_summaries_ood_rate_overall
```

@fig-data-summaries-ood-rate-district-scatterplot displays the relationship between in- and out-of-district contribution amounts, for each electoral district present in our dataset. We display donations to candidates and district associations separately. In both cases, out-of-district contribution rates vary greatly from district to district[^marginal-OOD-distribution]. Some Toronto metropolitan districts such as Toronto---St. Paul's and University---Rosedale sent between 70% and 80% of their contributions to localized entities in other districts, while others such as Alberta's Lethbridge and Ontario's Niagara Falls only sent between 5% and 15% of their localized contribution sum to other districts. Many districts, especially for donations addressed to candidates, have low out-of-district donation rates, as is illustrated by the line of points near $y = 0$ in @fig-data-summaries-ood-rate-district-scatterplot. We also find that, at least among the few top districts by contribution amount, out-of-district propensity is not a simple function of urbanization; Vancouver Granville in British Columbia and Brampton North in Ontario are similarly metropolitan, but have very different out-of-district contribution rates to electoral candidates. District-level differences in candidate-bound out-of-district contribution rates are even more pronounced when election periods are examined individually (Supplement {{< meta supp.extra-viz >}}.).

[^marginal-OOD-distribution]: The marginal distribution of out-of-district proportions across all districts is shown in Supplement {{< meta supp.extra-viz >}}.

Points represent individual districts, and are colored based on the share of funds sent to (A) district associations or (B) candidates in other districts. The top 3 districts by amount contributed in- and out-of-district respectively are labelled. Graphs are similar when donor counts are displayed instead of aggregated donation amount. Subplot B looks similar when specific election cycles are considered. The grey dashed line is 1:1."
```{r}
#| fig-height: 6

district_totals <- localized_donations_data %>%

    in_district = sum(total_amount[!is_out_of_district]) / 1000,
    out_district = sum(total_amount[is_out_of_district]) / 1000,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ood_scatter <- function(entity, panel_name) {
  d <- filter(district_totals, political_entity == entity)
  labels <- bind_rows(slice_max(d, in_district, n = 3), slice_max(d, out_district, n = 3))
  ggplot(d, aes(in_district, out_district)) +
    geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "black") +
    geom_point(aes(colour = out_district / (in_district + out_district)), size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_text(data = labels, aes(label = donor_district), size = 2, vjust = -0.6, check_overlap = TRUE) +
    scale_colour_gradient(
      name = "% out-of-district",
      low = "grey60", high = "#4169E1",
      limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = scales::label_percent(),

    ) +
    labs(
      x = "In-District Total ($ Thousands)",
      y = "Out-of-District Total ($ Thousands)",

    ) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(

      legend.title = element_text(size = 5),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 4),
      plot.title   = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
    )
}

p1 <- ood_scatter("Registered associations", "A. District Associations (Sum from 2015 to 2024)")
p2 <- ood_scatter("Candidates", "B. Candidates (Sum of 42nd, 43rd, and 44th Elections)")
```

### Spatial Reach of Out-of-district Donations {#sec-data-summaries-ood-network}

<!-- TODO: UPDATE THE REVIEW RESPONSE SAYING I MADE THESE CHANGES HERE. ALSO STATE THAT TALK OF "TRAVEL" WAS CUT DOWN FROM RESULTS SECTION AS WELL.  -->
Our final set of data summaries focus on the out-of-district donations themselves, examining their "reach". @tbl-data-summaries-ood-neighbours shows the proportion of out-of-district contributions bound for neighbouring districts, and districts in other provinces or territories. For both candidates and EDAs, around 40% of out-of-district donations are sent to adjacent districts, and only around 12% are sent to other provinces. Overall, out-of-district donations are received in districts closer to home for candidate-bound donations, echoing findings from @tbl-data-summaries-ood-rate-overall. For the interested reader, we provide a visualization of inter-provincial donation networks in Supplement {{< meta supp.extra-viz >}}.

A more granular picture of how far typical out-of-district donations reach is shown in @fig-ood-distance-distribution, illustrating the distribution of donor--recipient distances[^distance-calculation]. Most out-of-district donations are  received in districts about a far away from the donor as the average distance between two metropolitan districts (green vertical line). Out-of-district donations that are sent farther than this are relatively uncommon, and become extremely rare past 1000km. Two exceptions are donations with donor--recipient distances of around 2700 and 3400 kilometres. These observations correspond primarily to donations between Toronto and Calgary, and between Toronto and Vancouver respectively. Taken together, these summaries suggest that out-of-district donations are largely regionalized, and, for the most part, contained within their province of origin. The few donations sent beyond the donor's provincial boundary mainly consist of donations between large metropolitan centres.

[^distance-calculation]: The donor--recipient distance of an out-of-district donation was taken to be the Haversine great-circle distance between the centroid coordinates of the donor's dissemination area and the centroid coordinates of the recipient's district.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-data-summaries-ood-neighbours
#| tbl-cap: "Proportion of out-of-district contributions over $200 that were sent to adjacent districts, and out-of-province during our study period."

# Create Table
Tbl_data_summaries_ood_neighbours <- localized_donations_data_neighbours %>%
  filter(is_out_of_district) %>%
  mutate(`Received by` = ifelse(political_entity == "Candidates", "Candidate", "District association")) %>%
  group_by(`Received by`) %>%
  summarise(
    `Adjacent district.By count` = mean(are_neighbors),
    `Adjacent district.By amount` = sum(are_neighbors * total_amount) / sum(total_amount),
    `Out-of-province.By count` = mean(is_out_of_province),
    `Out-of-province.By amount` = sum(is_out_of_province * total_amount) / sum(total_amount),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(-`Received by`, names_to = c("Sent to", ".value"), names_sep = "\\.") %>%
  mutate(
    `By count` = scales::percent(`By count`, accuracy = 0.1),
    `By amount` = scales::percent(`By amount`, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) %>%
  tinytable::tt(width = 1) %>%
  format_tt(escape = TRUE) %>%
  style_tt(j = 1:4, align = "llrr") %>%
  style_tt(i = 0:nrow(.), fontsize = 0.85) %>%
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)

Tbl_data_summaries_ood_neighbours
```

## Regression Model Specifications {#sec-model-specification}
<!--
      - Propensity Model                UOA: Pr(is_out_of_district)                 PURPOSE: characterization            
      - Candidate Model                 UOA: Pr(is_out_of_district)                 PURPOSE: motivation HT    
-->

### Individual-Level Model {#sec-model-specification-individual}

<!-- TODO: BIG DECISION TO STATE IN THE REVIEW RESPONSE: THE DISTRICT-LEVEL MODEL WAS MOVED TO THE SUPPLEMENT. THIS WAS DONE TO MAKE ROOM FOR THE CANDIDATE-FOCUSED MODEL. WE FEEL THAT THE READER IS NOT IMPACTED AS THE RESULTS LARGELY AGREED WITH THE INDIVIDUAL MODEL, AND THEY ARE BOTH GETTING AT THE IDEA OF PROPENSITY. WHAT THE SECOND MODEL BROUGHT SUBSTANTIALLY WAS  --> 

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| label: individual-ood-propensity-model

individual_model <- glm(
  is_out_of_district ~
    political_entity +
    political_party_cat +
    total_amount +
    donor_region +
    avg_age +
    median_hh_income +
    postsec_prop +
    vismin_total +
    margin_of_victory_avg +
    density_per_sqkm_sqrt,
  data = individual_model_data,
  family = "binomial"
)
```

We used a logistic regression model to explore how the likelihood of out-of-district donation varies across different transactional characteristics, donor demographic environments, and district competitiveness, for individual donations. Our outcome variable is binary: whether or not a donation was sent out-of-district. This model was fit on both donations to EDAs and candidates together. Models fit on each entity separately had similar coefficient magnitudes, signs and significances (Supplement {{< meta supp.alt-models >}}). Donations were not grouped by individual, since we were interested in both donor and recipient characteristics in this model. Diagnostics showed that residual autocorrelation, the primary statistical risk associated with this decision, was negligible.

The transactional predictors in our model are: the type of recipient (candidate or district association), their political party, and the monetary value of the donation. We did not include time-indexed variables since our data summaries showed that out-of-district rates were constant over time, for both candidates and district associations. Following @garnett_where_2024 and @gimpel_political_2006, we also considered the following characteristics of the donor's socio-demographic environment: province (grouped into regions), mean age, median household income, the share of the population with a post-secondary degree, and the share of the population that is a visible minority[^visible-minority-disaggregation], at the dissemination level. These are characteristics of the donor's residential environment rather than of the donor themselves. As such, this model speaks to the types of places (rather than the types of people) from which out-of-district donations come. District competitiveness was proxied using the difference between the percentage of votes received by the winning and runner-up candidates, averaged across all three general elections captured in our study period, inspired by @garnett_where_2024. This predictor was included since we might expect donors from less competitive districts to donate out-of-district more often, perhaps recognizing that a local contribution will do little to affect an outcome that is effectively predetermined.

We also included the population density of the donor’s district, for two reasons. First, out-of-district donors are more likely to come from urban (and therefore more densely populated) districts in the U.S. [@gimpel_political_2006]. Second, population density serves as a relatively good proxy for how spatially clustered a district is, since Canadian districts are designed to have similar population sizes [@canada_redistribution_2025], and for the urban--rural character of a district, which has been found to matter in Canadian federal elections [@armstrong_urbanrural_2022]. Out-of-district donation rates are likely naturally higher in geographically smaller districts, since donors are more likely to interact with individuals, businesses, or politicians close by that happen to be located in a different district. Population density was transformed in the model by applying a square root, allowing us to interpret the metric as the inverse of the average distance between people,capturing this distance effect more faithfully.

The resulting model is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{logit}(p_i) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Election}_i + \beta_2 \text{Candidate}_{i} + \sum_{j=3}^{5} \beta_j \text{Party}_{ji} + \beta_6 \text{Amount}_i \\
&\quad + \sum_{k=7}^{11} \beta_k \text{Region}_{ki} + \beta_{12} \text{Age}_i + \beta_{13} \text{Income}_i + \beta_{14} \text{Education}_i + \beta_{15} \text{VisMin}_i \\
&\quad + \beta_{16} \text{VictoryMargin}_i + \beta_{17} \text{Density}_i \\
\end{aligned}
$$

where:

- $p_i$ is the probability that donation $i$ was an out-of-district donation.
- $\text{Election}_i$ indicates whether donation $i$ occurred during a general election period.
- $\text{Candidate}_{i}$ indicates whether donation $i$ was addressed to a Candidate (baseline is EDA).
- $\text{Party}_{ji}$ indicates recipient party affiliation for donation $i$ (among Liberal, N.D.P, or Other, with baseline being Conservative).
- $\text{Amount}_i$ is the monetary value of donation $i$, in thousands of dollars.
- $\text{Region}_{ki}$ indicates which region (among Atlantic Canada, B.C., Prairies, Quebec, Territories, with baseline being Ontario) the donor is located.
- $\text{Age}_i$ is the average age of residents in the donor's dissemination area.
- $\text{Income}_i$ is the median household income in the donor's dissemination area, in thousands of dollars.
- $\text{Education}_i$ is the proportion of residents in the donor's dissemination are holding a post-secondary qualification.
- $\text{VisMin}_i$ is the proportion of residents in the donor's dissemination area who identify as a visible minority.
- $\text{VictoryMargin}_i$ is the difference between the percentage of votes received by the winning and runner-up candidates, averaged across all three general elections in the donor's home district.
- $\text{Density}_i$ is the square root of the population density of the donor's dissemination area.

[^visible-minority-disaggregation]: An alternative model where the visible minority proportion was disaggregated into specific ethnic groups is shown in Supplement {{< meta supp.alt-models >}}.

<!-- KEEPSAKE: Districts were more likely to have elected an MP from the same party (or simply the same MP) for all three elections when their average margin of victory is higher ($\text{pseudo} \space R^2 = 0.22$), meaning that this competitiveness metric also captures a decent share of the variation in district-level party stability. -->

### Recipient-Based Model {#sec-model-specification-recipient}

<!-- What is the goal of this model?:
      - To establish that the only characteristic of candidates/races per se that increases OOD propensity is ethnicity. From this I can say that ethnic candidates are definitely attracting more out-of-district donors.  
      - Margin of victory effect dissapeared in the presence of demographic characteristics.
      - We also identified a strong interaction effect between the source vismin proportion and this candidate effect.
 -->

The primary goal of the first model was to model out-of-district propensity at their source across space. Here we fit a final model with the goal of better understanding the types of candidates and races that receive out of district donations. Like with the individual variable, our outcome variable is whether or not a donation was sent out-of-district. 

The resulting model is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{logit}(p_i) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Ethnicity}_j + \beta_2 \text{Gender}_j + \beta_3 \text{Incumbency}_j + \beta_4 \text{LGBTQ2S}_j \\ 
&\quad + \beta_5 \text{VictoryMargin}_k + \eta_{ij} + u_j + v_k \quad \\ \\
&\quad  u_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2_u), \quad v_k \sim N(0, \sigma^2_v)
\end{aligned}
$$

where: 
- $\text{Ethnicity}_j$ indicates whether candidate $j$ is white.
- $\text{Gender}_j$ indicates whether candidate $j$ is male.
- $\text{Incumbency}_j$ indicates whether candidate $j$ was an incumbent during their race.
- $\text{LGBTQ2S}_j$ indicates whether candidate $j$ is out as LGBTQ2S. 
- $\text{VictoryMargin}_k$ indicates the margin of victory of race $k$.
- $\eta_{ijk}$ represents every covariate used to fit the district model (acting as controls in this model).
- $u_j$ and $v_k$ represent random intercepts for candidates and races respectively.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| label: recipient-ood-propensity-model

# Temp Note: `recipient_model_data` is just the result of scripts/cleaning/06. When I'm done fiddling with the model, update 06 to only include exactly those variables that appear in my final model.

recipient_model_full <- glmmTMB(
  is_out_of_district ~
    # focal covariates
    candidate_ethnicity +
    candidate_gender +
    candidate_incumbency +
    candidate_out_LGBTQ2S +
    destination_margin_of_victory +
    destination_margin_of_victory_lag +
    # confounding variables: socio-demographic characteristics of destination district 
    destination_region +
    destination_avg_age +
    destination_median_hh_income +
    destination_postsec_prop +
    destination_vismin_total + 
    sqrt(destination_density_per_sqkm) +
    # confounding variables: other
    candidate_party +
    total_amount +
    # data structure
    (1 | election_year:destination_district) + (1 | candidate_ID),
  data = recipient_model_data_noIndigenous,
  family = binomial
)

recipient_model_affinity_effect <- glmmTMB(
  is_out_of_district ~
    # focal covariates
    candidate_ethnicity +
    candidate_gender +
    candidate_incumbency +
    candidate_out_LGBTQ2S +
    destination_margin_of_victory +
    destination_margin_of_victory_lag +
    candidate_ethnicity * source_vismin_total +
    # confounding variables: socio-demographic characteristics of destination district 
    destination_region +
    destination_avg_age +
    destination_median_hh_income +
    destination_postsec_prop +
    destination_vismin_total + 
    sqrt(destination_density_per_sqkm) +
    # confounding variables: socio-demographic characteristics of source district (THIS IS A LITTLE SILLY)
    # source_region +
    # source_avg_age +
    # source_median_hh_income +
    # source_postsec_prop +
    # source_vismin_total + 
    # sqrt(destination_density_per_sqkm) +
    # confounding variables: other
    candidate_party +
    total_amount +
    # data structure
    (1 | election_year:destination_district) + (1 | candidate_ID),
  data = recipient_model_data,
  family = binomial
)
summary(recipient_model_affinity_effect)

```

# Results {#sec-results}

Here we present the results from our fitted regression models. We note that many of our key findings are best understood as data summaries and visualizations, which are presented in @sec-data-summaries. @sec-data-summaries-situation provides context for how the localized contributions considered in our study fit into the broader scope of financial contributions in general. @sec-data-summaries-ood-rate provides spatio-temporal summaries of out-of-district propensity (which were used to inform the models discussed here). @sec-data-summaries-ood-network briefly characterizes the spatial reach of out-of-district donations. Both summary-based and model-based findings are discussed together in @sec-discussion.

<!-- Explaining how the models should be interpreted. -->
Regression results from the out-of-district propensity model are presented in @tbl-results-model-propensity and @fig-results-model-propensity. provide a visualization of coefficient signs, magnitudes, and significances. For both models, exponentiating the coefficients yields a more interpretable value, the odds ratio. For the individual (i.e. logistic) regression model, an odds ratio above one for a categorical variable (e.g. recipient belonging to the Liberal Party) indicates that, holding all else constant, donations of that category have increased odds of being out-of-district, relative to the baseline category (e.g. recipient belonging to the Conservative party). For the district level (i.e. beta) regression model, an odds ratio above one for a categorical variable (e.g. district situated in the Prairies) indicates that, holding all else constant, the expected ratio of out- vs. in-district contributions increases. Odds ratios less than one and continuous variables (e.g. median household income) are interpreted accordingly.

<!-- Walking through basic findings of the propensity model. -->
Donations over \$200 are less likely to be sent out-of-district when they are bound for candidates instead of district associations (EDAs). Out-of-district propensity is higher when the donation is addressed to a Liberal instead of a Conservative recipient, however differences between Conservative and N.D.P recipients were insignificant. Larger donations were more likely to leave the district compared to smaller ones, helping to explain why amount-weighted proportions in our data summaries were consistently larger than count-based proportions. The average margin of victory (taken to be a measure of district non-competitiveness) was, expectedly, positively associated with out-of-district propensity. Donations originating from all regions were less likely to be be sent out-of-district compared to Ontario, with the exception of Quebec, whose donors have nearly 1.5 times the odds to donate out-of-district, holding all else constant. Donors originating in the Territories were especially unlikely to donate outside their district, with nearly one-eighth the baseline Ontario odds. Turning to the donor's socio-demographic environment, higher population densities, post-secondary education rates, median household incomes, and visible minority proportions[^brampton-removal] all favoured out-of-district donation. However, the average age did not significantly impact out-of-district chances in the presence of other socio-demographic variables. When ethnicities were disaggregated, the positive effect of the visible minority proportion was observed for all minority ethnic groups recorded in the Census (Supplement {{< meta supp.alt-models >}}).

<!-- Commenting on the explanatory power of  -->


The eight variables used in our district-level model were able to explain a large amount of the variance in the ratio of out- to in-district donation (${pseudo} \space R^2 = 0.67$). The same model fit on only population density also achieved a relatively good fit (${pseudo} \space R^2 = 0.45$), however other variables, and especially socio-demographic ones such as educational attainment and visible minority proportion, improved the model's explanatory power well past what population density alone could offer.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

<!-- Intro -->
In this paper, we used publicly available political financing data to document the extent and spatio-temporal trends in Canadian out-of-district donations from 2015 to 2024. Further, we identify environmental characteristics associated with out-of-district propensity, quantify the reach of these donations, and provide an initial look at the spatial network formed by out-of-district donations. Our findings are also contextualized within the broader scope of all Canadian federal political contributions over $200 during this time (see @sec-data-summaries-situation). We present and discuss our major findings here, along with some notable study limitations.

<!-- Donation amount varies over time, OOD doesn't. -->
During our study period, out-of-district donations made up a large share of all donations received by localized political entities (electoral candidates and district associations). Naturally, donation rates to these two political entities varied through time; campaign funding was restricted to election periods, and donations to district associations swelled in December of each year and during electoral cycles, bringing in nearly five times more contributions compared to baseline rates. The share of funding received from outside their district, however, remained relatively constant throughout the decade: roughly 40% of individual donations over $200, accounting for 44% of the total amount contributed. This rate and its consistency through time contrasts against U.S. findings, where the bulk of existing out-of-district donations research has been done. There, out-of-district funding shares to senators and congressional representatives during electoral campaigns have increased since the start of the 21st century [@gimpel_political_2006; @canes_wrone_out_2022; @sievert_out_2023], and the average representative in 2016 received around two-thirds of their contributions from out-of-district [@gimpel_check_2008; @canes_wrone_out_2022].

<!-- Districts vary enormously in their out-of-district propensity, more than what you might expect from passive diffusion. -->
While out-of-district contribution rates varied little over time, across parties, and between localized entities, we observed drastic differences in rates from district-to-district. For example, out-of-district donation shares to district associations over the entire studied decade were as little as 5% for some districts (e.g. Niagara Falls), and as high as 75% in others (e.g. Toronto --- St. Paul's). While we might expect passively higher out-of-district rates solely due to the spatial proximity of other districts, empirical variation in rates of out-of-district giving (aggregated at the district level) far exceeded simulated expectations under this hypothesis. Further, most deviations from expected out-of-district donation rates were districts with higher than expected out-of-district contribution shares (Supplement {{< meta supp.distance-sim >}}). Also, this variation is not simply reflective of differences in the total amount each district gives; restricting our sample to only those districts among the top 10% by total contributed amount yielded a similarly broad range of out-of-district propensities.

<!-- There are clear socio-demographic predictors of OOD, especially VMP, attributable to two plausible mechanisms. -->
Donations originating from more densely populated, higher-income, and better-educated districts are more likely to travel out-of-district, all else held constant. These findings agree with the profile of the "donor districts" identified in the U.S. [@gimpel_check_2008], and with the predictors of donation propensity across North America in general [@gimpel_political_2006; @gimpel_check_2008; @garnett_where_2024]. By contrast, the visible minority proportion of a donor's home environment is positively associated with out-of-district propensity, departing from the historically white profile of American "donor districts" [@gimpel_check_2008]. Recent Canadian studies support this inverted relationship between ethnicity and political engagement. @garnett_lifeblood_2022, among others, note that some minority populations such as South Asians donate at rates which far exceed their share of the population, and, topically, @besco_ethnic_2022 found that individual donors belonging to most minority ethnic groups show higher rates of out-of-district donation compared to donors of European descent. The strong relationship between highly minoritized regions of the country and rates of out-of-district giving identified in our study is most plausibly attributed to one of two mechanisms which our models, as specified, cannot disentangle: demographic collinearity, and individual co-ethnic affinity. First, the relationship may simply reflect Canada’s unique social demography. Here, visible minority populations are concentrated almost exclusively in cities [@hou_recent_2004], and higher minority composition is not obviously associated with lower income at the national level [@walks_ghettos_2006]. In the U.S., however, visible minority proportion does not closely follow an urban-rural gradient [@lee_ethnoracial_2017], and these areas do have lower income, on average [@quillian_segregation_2012]. Therefore, our visible minority covariate may be absorbing residual features of affluent, dense, urban Canada that density and income alone do not fully capture, rather than reflecting effects of ethnicity per se. Alternatively, this relationship may be signalling the presence of out-of-district co-ethnic donations. Identity-based donor affinity is a well-established feature of Canadian political participation [@besco_identities_2019;  @besco_ethnic_2022; @tolley_who_2022]. Further, the largest component of our inter-district donation network we could identify is the flow of funds between the four districts that make up the Brampton region within the Greater Toronto Area, whose population is majority South Asian. While attractive, this hypothesis cannot be confirmed without individualized ethnic identification data, which is largely inaccessible at this scale. Our results are at a district-level not individual.

<!-- OOD is ultimately a regionalized phenomnon => local campaigns source their funding within their own province. -->
Despite empirically non-trivial rates of out-of-district donation, our study provides evidence that these donations remain a largely regionalized phenomenon. Nearly half of donations that leave their district during our study period were destined for entities in adjacent ones, and only around 12% ever even left their donor's province (in particular, 9% for candidate-bound donations). U.S. research on out-of-state donations describes highly nationalized donor bases among incumbent and campaigning House representatives [@gimpel_political_2006; @canes_wrone_out_2022; @sievert_out_2023; @keena_out_2024]. For example, a study on Senate elections from 2000 to 2020 found that both Republican and Democrat senators received, respectively, 60% and 49% of their donations from out-of-state during election periods [@sievert_out_2023]. The spatial proximity of U.S. states relative to Canadian provinces and territories may explain some of this difference, but its scale speaks to a more fundamental difference between the geographical donor bases of each country. The typical localized political entity in Canada sources donor-based funding largely from within their own province. In terms of thinking about local representation in Canada, our results are perhaps reassuring. For the most part donors are within or adjacent to the communities that the recipients want to represent. Further research should examine whether more complex patterns exist in this donor network, such as the clear divide between sender and receiver districts displayed in Supplement {{< meta supp.extra-viz >}}. Further research should also examine which candidates receive out-of-district funds. Publicly available datasets on Canadian federal candidates [@sevi_who_2021; @johnson_dataset_2021; @baisley_lgbtq_2025] would allow the exploration of the relationship between district funding and candidate gender, race, Indigenous background, and sexuality.

<!-- Data Limitation: Missing donations under $200, which form a non-ignorable proportion  of localized donations. -->
Our findings are accompanied by some important limitations. Following @gimpel_check_2008 and @garnett_where_2024, donations under \$200 (34% of the total amount sent to localized entities) were excluded from our study. The majority (75%) of exclusions were donations whose donors did not disclose their location. Comparisons between these contributions and those used in our study (Supplement {{< meta supp.missing-data >}}.) showed that they were similarly distributed across recipient characteristics such as party affiliation, region, and over time, suggesting that their exclusion introduced little systematic bias into our study dataset. However, 25% of donations under \$200 were location-disclosed (8.5% of the total), and were distributed quite differently. To an overwhelming degree, these were in-district donations to Liberal district associations outside of election cycles. Further investigation revealed that only 12.4% of these transactions had a unique donor name, postal code and year, against 92.7% in our study data, suggesting that most come from donors whose annual total contributions exceeded the $200 disclosure threshold [@canada_annual_2026]. Their exclusion therefore likely inflates our out-of-district estimates for Liberal district associations, already the highest of any entity-party pair (57% against a 40% average). More generally, this finding, paired with the positive association between amount donated and out-of-district propensity, suggests that our estimates of out-of-district donation rates (particularly the amount-unweighted point estimates) are overestimating the true underlying out-of-district propensity. Nevertheless, since contributions under \$200 remained similarly distributed to the study data, particularly in space, their exclusion is unlikely to have qualitatively affected the fitted coefficients of the most interesting covariates in our out-of-district propensity models, including those related to social demography.

<!-- Conceptual Limitation: Donor-based funding is only one side of the campaign funding story. -->
More conceptually, studying out-of-district contributions meant restricting our focus to contributions sent directly from donors to localized political entities, precluding other essential pathways that govern campaign finance broadly. The most important of these excluded funding pathways are contributions to national parties and intra-party transfers. As shown in @sec-data-summaries, most (~ 80%) contributions above \$200 are received by national parties or leadership contestants, and roughly 50% of the time during general election periods. Because transfers limit the financial leverage of direct individual donations, the regionalization of donor bases we identify cannot be read as evidence that the overall funding of these entities is regionalized: in principle, localized entities may be routinely funded by party transfers originally sourced from donors thousands of kilometres away. Despite this, direct individual contributions are clearly an essential pathway for the financing of many local campaigns [@cross_money_2020; @garnett_where_2024], especially when taking into account contributions to district associations [@cross_money_2020], which we do. Given the prevalence of individual donations to national parties, and the essential part they play in local campaign financing, further research should investigate whether national party donor bases are mostly constrained to particular regions of the country, as has been found in U.S. research. Our accessible dataset of donor-geolocated contributions is well-positioned to answer this question.
